newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Saudi dissident moves to Afghanistan's Kandahar.
newsitem.headline: Saudi dissident moves to Afghanistan's Kandahar.

text.p: The Taleban administration confirmed on Thursday that Saudi Arabian dissident Osama bin Laden, who is living in Afghanistan, had moved to the southern city of Kandahar, the Taleban's decision-making centre.

Bin Laden, who was stripped of his Saudi nationality in 1994, is wanted by the United States and Saudi Arabian authorities in connection with two bombings in Saudi Arabia that killed 24 U.S. servicemen and two Indian nationals.
Afghanistan's acting Information Minister Amir Khan Mutaqi said the move by bin Laden, who had settled in the eastern Afghan city of Jalalabad, was a personal decision.
"Osama bin Laden is in Kandahar. Going to Kandahar was a personal decision of bin Laden's," Mutaqi told journalists in Kabul.
Bin Laden's move was earlier reported by the Saudi-owned newspaper al-Hayat.
"Kandahar is the decision-making centre of the Taleban movement, and if bin Laden wants to discuss anything with the Taleban, he can go and see the leader directly," said Mutaqi.
Bin Laden is campaigning to remove Western troops from Saudi Arabia, which contains Islam's two holiest cities.
Bin Laden settled in Jalalabad after being forced to leave Sudan. The Taleban say he is a guest and will not be forced to leave.
"Bin Laden is a guest of the Afghans and he will be treated as a guest. There is no pressure for him to leave the country," said Mutaqi.
Mutaqi said earlier that bin Laden would not be allowed to carry out "terrorist" activities from Afghan soil.

"We are hospitable people," he said. "But we will not allow Afghanistan to be used to launch terrorist attacks. The Taleban will never allow bin Laden to use Afghan territory for training camps or subversive acts against any other country."

He said he did not know if the subject of bin Laden would arise in a meeting to be held between the head of the Taleban's interim ruling council, Mullah Mohammed Rabbani, and King Fahd of Saudi Arabia on April 14.
The Taleban, who captured Kabul last September and control about 75 percent of Afghanistan, have yet to be recognised as the legitimate government by any nation or international body.
